newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Funds go hunting African "lions".
newsitem.headline: Funds go hunting African "lions".

text.p: For many investors, familiar with buying shares in South Africa's gold mines or industrial companies, Africa stops at the country's border.
But a growing band of emerging market funds are beginning to hunt for value in the rest of sub-Saharan Africa, lured by privatisations and some very cheap assets.
John Clemmow, of Investec Securities in Johannesburg, says there has been an explosion of interest in Africa this year, although in global terms the flows remain tiny.
"Africa is still a specialist field. It's still not on the horizon for the general emerging market investor, but there are a lot more people who are interested," he said.
Part of the reason was the spectacular performance last year of the Zimbabwe Stock Exchange (ZSE) where the industrial index soared 90 percent in dollar terms.

The dismal record of the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), which sank to the bottom of the emerging market league table in the wake of last year's rand crisis, has also tempted more investors to look north.
"There is definitely growing demand from foreign funds," said Tom Minney, general manager of the Namibian Stock Exchange.
"We are past the stage where people are only looking at South Africa. Our stockbrokers are putting out a lot more research to places like New York and London."
Zimbabwe aside, Kenya -- where the privatisation of Kenya Airways kick-started foreign interest in March 1996 -- and Mauritius are the only other markets with comparable liquidity.

But despite sluggish trade, the stock markets in Ivory Coast, Ghana and Nigeria have also seen an increase in foreign interest this year, as have the smaller southern Africa exchanges of Namibia and Botswana.

Economists said these African markets were benefiting from economic reforms, albeit somewhat patchy, coupled with better commodity prices and recent good rains. Prices have risen, but markets continue to offer historic price/earnings ratios in the low teens.
For the determined Africa bulls, however, the real bargains lie in still more junior stock markets -- some of which have yet to open their doors for trading.
"At the beginning of the life cycles of these markets the valuations are so cheap they are really compelling," said Hania Farhan, Africa economist at investment bank ING Barings.

Clemmow argues that while African countries may lack the infrastructure to match the "tiger" economies of Asia, recent reforms may lead to a new breed of African "lions" with growth rates of six percent plus.

"The larger funds are looking at places like Kenya, Mauritius and to a lesser extent West Africa. But the ones who are really scenting value are looking to places like Zambia, Tanzania, Uganda and Malawi, some of whose stock markets are only going to be opening later this year," he said.

Zambia, where privatisation will take a quantum leap forward with the sale of the Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines this year, could be the world's top-performing emerging market in 1997, Clemmow believes.

Charles Mate, general manager of the Lusaka Stock Exchange, said the first foreign interest in Zambian stocks came with last year's privatisation listing of Zambia Sugar, and since then more overseas buyers have been dipping their toes in the market.

"Last year we saw significant participation from U.S., British and Swiss funds which saw turnover jump tenfold, and it should continue this year with a lot of interest in the listing of Zambia Breweries in June," he said.
Some apparently remarkable bargains still remain.
Tobacco monopoly Rothmans Zambia, for example, has $7 million in the bank but a market capitalisation of only $5 million, and a price/earnings ratio of under three.
Elsewhere, Malawi, with just two listed stocks, has yet to get off the starting blocks in attracting investors.

But Tanzania is already seeing some early-stage interest, even though the Dar es Salaam market will not open for several months. Tanzania Oxygen this month became the first company to submit its prospectus to the authorities. Others expected to follow include Tanzania Breweries and Tanzania Cigarette Co.
Analysts say the nascent stock markets of southern Africa could also get a boost from regional giant, South Africa, following changes to exchange control regulations announced in last month's budget.

That gave South African institutions extra leeway to invest in shares listed on stock exchanges in the 12-nation Southern African Development Community (SADC). Institutions will be allowed to invest 2 percent of their net 1996 inflows in SADC exchanges, including Zimbabwe, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia, Mauritius, Swaziland, Malawi and Tanzania.
